German authorities have revealed that Hamas was preparing a major terrorist attack against Jewish and Israeli targets in Europe, planned to coincide with the second anniversary of the October 7 massacre.

This was not merely propaganda, an online threat, or an early-stage fantasy.

The terrorists had reportedly selected a specific target, transported and stored weapons and ammunition, and even prepared a video claiming responsibility for the attack before it had taken place. Three suspects were arrested in Berlin on October 1, 2025 - only six days before the planned date. Further investigations led to six more arrests in Germany, Britain, Cyprus, and Denmark. 

Authorities also uncovered a Hamas-linked weapons cache in Vienna containing five handguns and ammunition. Investigators believe the weapons were intended for terrorist attacks against Jewish or Israeli institutions in Europe.

The media has described the plot as an attempted “second October 7.” We do not yet know whether the intended attack would have approached the horrifying scale of the massacre in Israel, but the evidence confirms that this was a serious, organized, multinational terrorist operation - not merely the work of a lone radical.

Even more disturbing is the fact that Hamas had reportedly begun establishing weapons caches and operational infrastructure across Europe years before October 7, 2023. German investigations indicate that Hamas commanders later ordered operatives to locate those weapons and prepare them for possible attacks. Other cells reportedly sought drones and cooperation with organized crime networks for attacks in Denmark or Sweden. 

Hamas has never been merely a “Palestinian resistance movement.”

It is an international Islamic terrorist organization whose hatred does not stop at Israel’s borders. Israel may be its first target, but the Jewish communities of Europe - and ultimately Europe itself - are also in its sights.

For years, European governments allowed Hamas supporters, financiers, propagandists, and sympathizers to operate under the protection of democratic freedoms. While crowds marched through European cities glorifying October 7 and calling for Israel’s destruction, Hamas was reportedly building the infrastructure for another massacre on European soil.

The chants were not harmless.

The demonstrations were not disconnected from the ideology of terrorism.

The weapons were real.

The targets were real.

And the attack was reportedly only days away when authorities intervened.

October 7 was not the end of Hamas’s ambitions. It was a model they hoped to export.

Europe must wake up before the next plot is not discovered in time.

David Sanger: “Trump Is Launching Now the Biggest War in the Middle East”

🔤🔤🔤🔤➖

Yemen’s Iranian-aligned Houthis have warned shipping companies that their tankers risk being attacked if they use Saudi Arabian ports, as the militia moved quickly to enforce a blockade announced the previous day.

The Houthi warning for the Red Sea, coming on top of Iran’s threat to shipping on the other side of the Arabian peninsular in the Gulf, could affect the substantial Saudi oil exports that have so far been unscathed by the months-long conflict and deepen the rapidly escalating crisis in the region.

Underlining how seriously the Houthi threat is being taken, three oil tankers that had loaded Saudi crude ⁠this week for China and India made U-turns on Tuesday away from Houthi-controlled coast at the mouth of the Red Sea and headed towards the Suez canal. The Houthis claimed six ships had changed course.

Donald Trump on Tuesday said the US would “​just have to ​take ‌care ​of ​business” if the Houthis followed through on their threats. 

“You know, we’ve done that with the Houthis before, and we haven’t heard from them in a while since we did what we did originally,” he said at White House meeting with the Lebanese president, Joseph Aoun.

The Houthi threat came as diplomats sought to salvage the collapsed interim deal between Iran and the US even as both countries continued to launch attacks in a 10th day of renewed fighting, including a visit to Pakistan by the Iranian interior minister, Eskandar Momeni, an important mediator in the conflict.

Sources suggested that behind the scenes there were indications that both sides might be seeking a way out of the latest round of intensive strikes. 

The news site Axios suggested that the Trump administration was weighing whether to escalate the conflict further or to seek a 10-day ceasefire to create the space for a new round of talks.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said Washington remained open to negotiating with Iran but that “it has to be real”.

The Houthis control ⁠northern Yemen, including territory along the Bab el-Mandeb, the strait at the southern end of the Red Sea.

🔔 Bitcoin price nears Fidelity’s power law support: Accumulation zone or missing catalyst? 

📌 On his power law model, a logarithmic chart that bounds Bitcoin’s entire price history between an upper resistance curve, a middle trendline, and a lower support curve, the floor currently sits near 58,000 dollars. That lower line has caught every major Bitcoin bottom since 2015. Timmer’s label for the zone the market has now entered is unambiguous: accumulation. His caveat is just as unambiguous: he sees no catalyst for a reversal, and he is not calling a bottom.

⚠️ That combination, a historically reliable floor approaching and a strategist refusing to ring the bell, is the most honest summary of the Bitcoin market in July 2026. The asset is coming off its worst quarter since the 2022 bear market, spot ETFs just recorded their largest quarterly outflow since launch, the speculative premium that carried the price past 120,000 dollars last year has evaporated, and the fast money has visibly rotated elsewhere, first into gold, then into semiconductor stocks. And yet the two quantitative measures Timmer trusts most, the deviation from the power law trendline and the Bitcoin-to-gold ratio, have both sunk to depths recorded at exactly two prior moments: the 2018 low and the 2022 low. Both of those moments were generational buying opportunities. Both also felt like the end of the world at the time.

🔖 This feature takes the model seriously in both directions: what the power law actually says, why its track record earns attention, and why the missing-catalyst objection is not a hedge but the core of the analysis.
